title: I vibe coded a free multiplayer FPS for the browser, playable on PC and phone
author: Inevitable_Salad_128
selftext:
When Opus 5.5 came out, I wanted to see what it can do in one shot. Then I kept iterating on that first result, and a few weeks later I have Riposte, a small multiplayer FPS in the browser, very inspired by the first Call of Duty games. 

  
[https://www.playriposte.com/](https://www.playriposte.com/)

Almost everything is code written by Claude Code, with three.js and no game engine. Weapons and maps are made in code, with very few external assets. I describe what I want in French, Claude makes the change and shows me screenshots from the game, then I test it myself on a dev version before it goes live.

I’m not a game dev, I just had a lot of fun (sometimes a little guilty) trying my ideas. What surprised me most is that small precise requests work way better than big ones. One time I asked to rework all the maps at once, it launched hundreds of agents for hours and burned my credits for almost nothing. Also the game feel (aim, recoil, sounds) took me much more time than adding features, and keeping the game light enough for phones was a constant fight.

It’s free and will stay free. I’m curious if some of you had the same experience, and what you think of the result.

replies.author: JayWelsh
replies.body: It’s not an unfair comparison because in the future we will see a lot more solo / low headcount dev studios. It will be easier to work on your own project than to find a decent job, so the “wage problem” goes away. Just my opinion.

replies.author: SilentNinja1337
replies.body: Definitely solo or small teams can make good games easier. But you shouldn't see your time as less worth, because it's your own project. If you spend 800 hours on a game, and then make 5000€ with it, that's not worth it. Even with just a salary of 20€/hr, you "loose"  11000€ you would have earned doing a normal SE job. Of course your personal satisfaction might be bigger creating games so that's okay for one.

replies.author: JayWelsh
replies.body: My position doesn’t involve seeing your time as less valuable, I’m not trying to say that, more that AI makes it easier for devs to “invest in themselves” to start their own projects in the hopes of potentially even better prospects than another SE job.

replies.author: Inevitable_Salad_128
replies.body: Thanks a lot! I actually planned to work on optimization soon, I also noticed some freezes on my side, so I add this to the feedback to fix. For the domain name, I just bought it directly on Vercel, for something like 10€ per year if I remember well. For the multiplayer part, Vercel is not enough, so I pay around 7€ per month for a small server on Hetzner, hosted in Germany, that runs the online lobbies

replies.author: JayWelsh
replies.body: Don’t make it like this (no offense to OP, it’s a really good outcome that they got, but there is massive room for improvement on the netcode side of things). Tell Claude Code to use Bevy as the game engine and then use something like Lightyear for your networking layer (Renet if you want to go more bear bones), and Avian for physics.

replies.author: dreamer_2142
replies.body:
Isn't the Op work the same as Epic online service (relay with punchthrough p2p connection)? That's what I gathered.  
I've been building my own relay system using LiteNetLib/udp, not that i know that much about, but codex was helping me. The ugly thing about it, it consumes a lot of bandwidth, unlike p2p.

replies.author: JayWelsh
replies.body:
It may be but using Node.js for this type of server is craycray from an efficiency and memory safety point of view. P2P tech is language agnostic. If you’re gonna vibecode a game then doing it in Rust is a good idea because it’s a language that LLMs are particularly good at using efficiently (plus the compiler/Clippy is very helpful with catching errors).

My suggested stack gives you a better chance at ending up with a high tick rate on the server. Nodejs is single threaded and will have a tough time coming close to competing with a Lightyear/Renet networking layer built in Rust.

You can still target browsers with your build if you use Bevy.

I’m actually tempted to suggest to OP to take their game and try to port it over to Bevy with a Lightyear/Renet networking layer. Their agent will be able to write better tests to catch regressions at compile time and their server tickrate will be able to be improved significantly. They have a great collection of mechanics & models and they have clearly put a lot of work into this, moving things over to a better stack would help their project scale a lot more.

replies.author: dreamer_2142
replies.body: I see, thanks for the explanation.

replies.author: JayWelsh
replies.body: It’s a pleasure, something I should have mentioned is that in contrast to Node’s single thread, Rust makes better use of your cores and can make your code more capable of parallelisation. It scales better and compiles strictly, which also happens to be great for the LLM driving it.

replies.author: Inevitable_Salad_128

With the current version of three.js it can even be slower on the CPU, and I would need to rewrite most of the rendering. It's also less safe on phones, which are my priority. What I got from it: the networking can clearly be improved, and I'm going to work on that first, without changing the whole tech stack. A full rewrite in Rust / Bevy sounds a bit overkill for where the project is today maybe? But I'm keeping the idea for later if the game ever needs to scale.
